title: The impurity of greed
hook: the impurity of the mind is greed, of the tongue lying (Asa di Var, ang 472)

segments.voice: Yesterday, compassion, and your line: it won't wear out. What quality did you name? Yesterday Guru Nanak looked inside a thread. Today he looks inside an old idea of being unclean. Day five hundred fifty-six.

Clean and dirty go deeper than germs. Shoes off at the door. Hands washed before eating. A kitchen counter nobody puts a bag on. Families and cultures draw those lines in different places, and they matter. In Guru Nanak's world, there was a strong idea called sootak: a time of ritual impurity that fell on a household after a birth or a death. For a set period, the family was considered unclean, and others might avoid their food. Guru Nanak took that word and asked where impurity really lives.
screen: `SHOES OFF AT THE DOOR.` → `SOOTAK: IMPURITY AFTER BIRTH OR DEATH.` → `WHERE DOES IMPURITY LIVE?`

segments.voice: The saloks are on ang 472, and they come in a short run. The first one starts with a practical puzzle. If you believe in sootak, it says, in paraphrase, then sootak is everywhere. There are tiny creatures in cow dung and in firewood. Not a single grain of food is without life. Water itself gives life to everything. So how can anyone keep sootak out? It's already in the kitchen. Then the salok's answer: Nanak, sootak isn't removed that way. Only spiritual wisdom washes it off. The next salok moves the word somewhere new. In paraphrase again: the sootak of the mind is greed. The sootak of the tongue is lying. Tomorrow we'll hear what it says about the eyes and the ears. For today, stay with those first two. Lobh, greed, is the mind's impurity: the restless wanting that never says enough. Koorh, the same word we met in the salok of the false king, is the tongue's. A household can follow every rule after a birth and still have a greedy mind at the table. A person can scrub their hands and still lie with their mouth. Guru Nanak isn't saying cleanliness doesn't matter; Sikh discipline includes bathing before the dawn prayers, and langar kitchens are kept clean. He's saying the impurity that really keeps people from the One isn't on the skin. A third salok finishes the thought: all sootak is doubt, attachment to something second. Birth and death come by the hukam, the divine order. They're not dirt. Greed and lying are.
screen: `SOOTAK: AN OLD IDEA OF IMPURITY.` · `LIFE IS IN EVERY GRAIN.` · `THE MIND'S IMPURITY: GREED.` · `THE TONGUE'S IMPURITY: LYING.` · then, large: `CLEAN TONGUE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep your tongue clean today. Sit and breathe. Rest your attention on your mouth for a moment: the tongue, the lips, the breath passing through. Then think ahead over today's conversations. Notice where a small untruth might slip out: an excuse, an exaggeration, a way of shading a story. Decide now, kindly, that today you'll let your words be plain and true. Let the tongue rest, quiet. If you pray, you can say Waheguru with that clean tongue. The bell holds the time.
Sootak. Ritual impurity, once thought to fall on a home after a birth or death. Guru Nanak moves it inside: the mind's sootak is greed, the tongue's is lying.
Your line: clean tongue. Today, catch one small exaggeration before it leaves your mouth, and say the plain version instead. Day five hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: Sikh practice keeps no period of ritual impurity after a birth or death; the Sikh Rehat Maryada sets such observances aside, and Sikhs hear these saloks in the dawn singing of Asa di Var.

trapdoor: what you thought: sootak is about dirt.
what it means: an old idea of ritual impurity that Guru Nanak moves inside: greed in the mind, lies on the tongue.
what a scholar hears: a run of saloks on ang 472 argues that life is in every grain and water, so outer sootak can't be kept out; only wisdom washes.

notes: Sootak described as a period of ritual impurity after birth (and, in some usage, death; patak/sutak distinctions exist); phrased as 'in Guru Nanak's world' without attributing to any present community. Confirm wording.
Three saloks paraphrased; confirm order, content and that all three are M1 on ang 472.
howItsDone: the Sikh Rehat Maryada rejects observances of impurity after birth/death; confirm the statement.
